title: Measurement and the Born Rule
intro: Measurement is where amplitudes become probabilities. It gives one random outcome per run, changes the state it measures, and so any expectation value must be estimated from many repetitions; this page teaches all three, from the Born rule to measuring in any basis and counting shots.

blocks.text: What you need first: States and Dirac Notation (#/quantum/foundations/states-and-dirac-notation) (kets, bras, inner products, the $X$ and $Y$ bases) and, for the sections on observables and degenerate outcomes, Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/quantum/foundations/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors). The section on shots uses the binomial distribution from Bernoulli, Binomial and Geometric (#/probability/distributions/binomial-and-geometric).
What you will be able to do

items: Compute the probability of every outcome of a measurement in any basis, and the state left behind afterwards.
Explain how a device that only measures in the computational basis can measure $X$ or $Y$, and work out the rotation it needs.
Compute an expectation value $\langle A\rangle$ two ways, from the outcome probabilities and as $\langle\psi\vert A\vert\psi\rangle$.
Handle measurements with degenerate outcomes and measurements of one qubit out of two.
Work out how many repetitions (shots) an experiment needs to estimate an expectation value to a given precision.

blocks.text: Why measurement needs its own rule

In classical physics, measuring something just reads off a value that was already there, and a careful enough measurement disturbs nothing. Quantum measurement breaks both habits. A qubit in the state $\alpha\vert0\rangle + \beta\vert1\rangle$ does not have a value of 0 or 1 waiting to be read (States and Dirac Notation (#/quantum/foundations/states-and-dirac-notation) shows an experiment that rules this out). When you measure it you get one outcome, at random, and afterwards the qubit is no longer in the state it was in. Two rules describe this: the Born rule says how likely each outcome is, and the collapse rule says what state is left. Everything else on this page, from measuring in other bases to estimating averages on a quantum computer, is those two rules applied carefully.
The Born rule

A measurement always comes with a basis: a set of orthonormal states $\{\vert e_k\rangle\}$, one for each possible outcome. Measuring a qubit in the computational basis has outcomes 0 and 1 with basis states $\vert0\rangle$, $\vert1\rangle$; measuring it in the $X$ basis has outcomes $+$ and $-$ with $\vert+\rangle$, $\vert-\rangle$. The Born rule says that if the system is in the state $\vert\psi\rangle$, the outcome $k$ occurs with probability

blocks.caption: The Born rule (Born 1926). The probabilities sum to 1 because the state is a unit vector.

blocks.text: In words: take the amplitude of $\vert\psi\rangle$ along the outcome's basis state, the inner product, and square its modulus. Max Born proposed the rule in 1926, in a footnote to a paper on collisions; it is not derived from anything else in quantum mechanics but is one of its postulates, tested in every experiment since.
Why the probabilities add to 1

They must, or the rule would be nonsense. Write $\vert\langle e_k\vert\psi\rangle\vert^2 = \overline{\langle e_k\vert\psi\rangle}\,\langle e_k\vert\psi\rangle = \langle\psi\vert e_k\rangle\langle e_k\vert\psi\rangle$, using the fact that swapping a bracket conjugates it. Then sum over $k$:

blocks.tex: \sum_k P(k) = \sum_k \langle\psi\vert e_k\rangle\langle e_k\vert\psi\rangle = \langle\psi\vert\Big(\sum_k\vert e_k\rangle\langle e_k\vert\Big)\vert\psi\rangle = \langle\psi\vert I\vert\psi\rangle = 1
blocks.caption: The resolution of the identity, then normalisation.

blocks.text: This is why states must be unit vectors and why the measurement basis must be orthonormal: together they make the probabilities a proper distribution.
Worked example: one state, three measurements
Use the state $\vert s\rangle = \sqrt{0.8}\,\vert0\rangle + i\sqrt{0.2}\,\vert1\rangle$ throughout this page. Its amplitudes are $0.8944$ and $0.4472i$.

items: Step 1. Computational basis: $\langle0\vert s\rangle = \sqrt{0.8}$ and $\langle1\vert s\rangle = i\sqrt{0.2}$. So $P(0) = 0.8$ and $P(1) = \vert i\vert^2\cdot0.2 = 0.2$.
Step 2. $X$ basis: $\langle\pm\vert s\rangle = (\sqrt{0.8} \pm i\sqrt{0.2})/\sqrt2$. The modulus squared of $a \pm ib$ with $a, b$ real is $a^2 + b^2$, so $P(+) = P(-) = (0.8 + 0.2)/2 = 0.5$.

Step 3. $Y$ basis: $\langle{\pm i}\vert = (\langle0\vert \mp i\langle1\vert)/\sqrt2$, so $\langle{+i}\vert s\rangle = (\sqrt{0.8} - i\cdot i\sqrt{0.2})/\sqrt2 = (\sqrt{0.8} + \sqrt{0.2})/\sqrt2$ and $\langle{-i}\vert s\rangle = (\sqrt{0.8} - \sqrt{0.2})/\sqrt2$.
Step 5. Each set adds to 1. The relative phase $i$ on $\vert1\rangle$ is invisible in $Z$ and $X$ but shows clearly in $Y$.

blocks.text: The Born rule with projectors
There is a second way to write the rule that generalises better. The projector onto outcome $k$ is $\Pi_k = \vert e_k\rangle\langle e_k\vert$, and

For the computational basis $\Pi_0 = \vert0\rangle\langle0\vert$ (rows $(1, 0)$, $(0, 0)$), and $\langle s\vert\Pi_0\vert s\rangle$ picks out $\vert s_0\vert^2 = 0.8$. This form is what you need once outcomes can be degenerate, later on this page.

blocks.title: Check yourself: Born rule
blocks.text: A qubit is in $\frac12\vert0\rangle - \frac{\sqrt3}{2}\vert1\rangle$. Find $P(0)$, $P(1)$ and $P(+)$.
blocks.hint: For $\vert+\rangle$, add the two amplitudes and divide by $\sqrt2$ before squaring.

blocks.text: Collapse: the state after a measurement
The second rule: if the outcome is $k$, the state immediately afterwards is $\vert e_k\rangle$, the basis state of the outcome. Whatever superposition there was is replaced.

blocks.alt: Flow diagram: the state alpha|0> + beta|1> enters a Z measurement box; with probability |alpha|^2 the outcome is 0 and the state becomes |0>, with probability |beta|^2 the outcome is 1 and the state becomes |1>.
blocks.caption: A computational-basis measurement: one random outcome per run, and the state is replaced by the matching basis state.

blocks.text: The clearest evidence is repeatability. Measure $\vert s\rangle$ in the computational basis and suppose you get 1 (probability 0.2). Measure again straight away, in the same basis: you get 1 again, with certainty, because the state is now $\vert1\rangle$ and $P(1) = \vert\langle1\vert1\rangle\vert^2 = 1$. A measurement that gave a different answer when repeated immediately would not be telling you about the system.
Measure in a different basis in between, though, and the first result is wiped out. Sequence: $Z$, then $X$, then $Z$ again.

items: Step 1. The first $Z$ gives, say, 0. The state is now $\vert0\rangle$.
Step 2. The $X$ measurement on $\vert0\rangle$: $P(+) = P(-) = \vert1/\sqrt2\vert^2 = 0.5$. Say it gives $+$; the state is now $\vert+\rangle$.
Step 3. The second $Z$ on $\vert+\rangle$: $P(0) = P(1) = 0.5$. The qubit has forgotten that it was 0.

Step 4. So the second $Z$ result disagrees with the first half the time, however carefully the $X$ measurement is done. Measuring $X$ disturbs $Z$; this is not a flaw of the apparatus but part of the theory, and it is the root of the uncertainty relations in Observables and Uncertainty (#/quantum/foundations/observables-and-uncertainty).

blocks.text: The code sample further down simulates exactly this: repeating $Z$ agrees in every run, while $Z$, $X$, $Z$ disagrees in about half of them.

What collapse is, physically, is one of the open questions about quantum mechanics (the measurement problem), and different interpretations answer it differently. For calculations it does not matter: every interpretation agrees on the two rules on this page. When the measuring device is treated as a quantum system too, collapse turns out to look like entanglement with the device followed by ignoring it; a later page of this shelf, on decoherence, shows how, building on Entanglement and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/entanglement).
Measuring in another basis with only one detector

Real qubit hardware, superconducting circuits or trapped ions, usually has one kind of detector: it tells you 0 or 1, a computational-basis ($Z$) measurement. Yet experiments routinely measure $X$ and $Y$. The trick is to rotate the state first, so that the basis you want lands on the computational basis, and then measure $Z$.
Why rotate-then-measure works

items: Step 1. Apply a unitary gate $U$ and then measure in the computational basis. By the Born rule the probability of outcome $k$ is $\vert\langle k\vert U\vert\psi\rangle\vert^2$.

Step 2. Move $U$ onto the bra. The bra of the ket $U^\dagger\vert k\rangle$ is $\langle k\vert U$, so $\langle k\vert U\vert\psi\rangle = \langle e_k\vert\psi\rangle$ with $\vert e_k\rangle = U^\dagger\vert k\rangle$.

Step 3. So the probability is $\vert\langle e_k\vert\psi\rangle\vert^2$: exactly the Born rule for a measurement in the basis $\{U^\dagger\vert k\rangle\}$. (These states are orthonormal because $U^\dagger$ is unitary and preserves inner products.)
Step 4. Recipe: to measure in the basis $\{\vert e_k\rangle\}$, find a unitary $U$ with $U\vert e_k\rangle = \vert k\rangle$, apply it, then measure $Z$.

blocks.text: Measuring X: a Hadamard first

The Hadamard gate $H_d$ (rows $(1, 1)/\sqrt2$ and $(1, -1)/\sqrt2$) takes $\vert+\rangle$ to $\vert0\rangle$ and $\vert-\rangle$ to $\vert1\rangle$. Check: $H_d\vert+\rangle = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}H_d(\vert0\rangle + \vert1\rangle) = \frac12\big((\vert0\rangle + \vert1\rangle) + (\vert0\rangle - \vert1\rangle)\big) = \vert0\rangle$. So outcome 0 after a Hadamard means $+$, and outcome 1 means $-$.

items: Step 1. Apply $H_d$ to $\vert s\rangle = \sqrt{0.8}\vert0\rangle + i\sqrt{0.2}\vert1\rangle$: $H_d\vert s\rangle = \sqrt{0.8}\,\frac{\vert0\rangle + \vert1\rangle}{\sqrt2} + i\sqrt{0.2}\,\frac{\vert0\rangle - \vert1\rangle}{\sqrt2}$.

Step 2. Collect terms: $H_d\vert s\rangle = \frac{\sqrt{0.8} + i\sqrt{0.2}}{\sqrt2}\vert0\rangle + \frac{\sqrt{0.8} - i\sqrt{0.2}}{\sqrt2}\vert1\rangle = (0.632 + 0.316i)\vert0\rangle + (0.632 - 0.316i)\vert1\rangle$.

Step 3. Measure $Z$: $P(0) = 0.632^2 + 0.316^2 = 0.5$. These are the $X$-basis amplitudes $\langle\pm\vert s\rangle$ from the worked example above, now sitting on $\vert0\rangle$ and $\vert1\rangle$. The rotation moved the amplitudes, not the probabilities.

blocks.text: Measuring Y: undo the phase, then a Hadamard

For $Y$ you need a $U$ with $U\vert{+i}\rangle = \vert0\rangle$. The phase gate $S$ is diagonal with entries $1$ and $i$, and its inverse $S^\dagger$ has entries $1$ and $-i$. $S^\dagger$ removes the $i$: $S^\dagger\vert{+i}\rangle = (\vert0\rangle + (-i)(i)\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2 = \vert+\rangle$. Then $H_d$ takes $\vert+\rangle$ to $\vert0\rangle$. So $U = H_dS^\dagger$: apply $S^\dagger$ first, then $H_d$ (in the product the gate applied first is written on the right).

items: Step 1. $S^\dagger\vert s\rangle = \sqrt{0.8}\vert0\rangle + (-i)(i)\sqrt{0.2}\vert1\rangle = \sqrt{0.8}\vert0\rangle + \sqrt{0.2}\vert1\rangle$. The phase is gone.
Step 2. $H_d$ of that: $\frac{\sqrt{0.8} + \sqrt{0.2}}{\sqrt2}\vert0\rangle + \frac{\sqrt{0.8} - \sqrt{0.2}}{\sqrt2}\vert1\rangle = 0.9487\vert0\rangle + 0.3162\vert1\rangle$.
Step 3. $P(0) = 0.9487^2 = 0.9$, which is $P(+i)$, as in the worked example. A $Y$ measurement is $S^\dagger$, $H_d$, then $Z$.

blocks.text: One subtlety. After the detector reports 0, the qubit is in $\vert0\rangle$, not in $\vert{+i}\rangle$. If you want the textbook post-measurement state you must undo the rotation ($U^\dagger = SH_d$) afterwards. Usually nobody bothers, because the qubit is reset or discarded after readout.

blocks.title: Check yourself: choose the rotation
blocks.text: Which single gate turns a $Z$-basis detector into a detector for the basis $\{\vert1\rangle, \vert0\rangle\}$ (outcome $a$ means $\vert1\rangle$, outcome $b$ means $\vert0\rangle$)? And what does applying $X$ before measuring do to the probabilities of $\vert s\rangle$?
solution: We need $U\vert1\rangle = \vert0\rangle$ and $U\vert0\rangle = \vert1\rangle$: that is the bit flip $X$.

$X\vert s\rangle = i\sqrt{0.2}\vert0\rangle + \sqrt{0.8}\vert1\rangle$, so the detector now reports $0$ with probability 0.2: it is reporting outcome $\vert1\rangle$ of the original state. Relabelling outcomes is the simplest change of basis.
blocks.answer: X; it swaps them to P(0) = 0.2, P(1) = 0.8

blocks.text: Measuring an observable, and expectation values

Physicists rarely say measure in the basis $\{\vert+\rangle, \vert-\rangle\}$. They say measure $X$, naming the observable: a Hermitian matrix whose eigenvalues are the numbers the dial can show and whose eigenvectors are the measurement basis. $X$ has eigenvalue $+1$ on $\vert+\rangle$ and $-1$ on $\vert-\rangle$, so measuring $X$ means measuring in the $X$ basis and reporting $+1$ or $-1$. In general an observable is written through its spectral decomposition (Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/quantum/foundations/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors)) as

blocks.caption: Outcomes a (the eigenvalues) and their projectors Π_a.

blocks.text: and the Born rule gives $P(a) = \langle\psi\vert\Pi_a\vert\psi\rangle$. The average result over many runs, the expectation value, is

blocks.caption: The expectation value: the probability-weighted average of the outcomes, which collapses into one bracket.

blocks.text: The last form is a shortcut: no eigenvectors needed, just one matrix-vector product and one inner product.
Worked example: the three Pauli expectations of the running state

items: Step 2. The same from the bracket: $Z\vert s\rangle = \sqrt{0.8}\vert0\rangle - i\sqrt{0.2}\vert1\rangle$, and $\langle s\vert Z\vert s\rangle = \sqrt{0.8}\cdot\sqrt{0.8} + \overline{(i\sqrt{0.2})}\cdot(-i\sqrt{0.2}) = 0.8 + (-i)(-i)(0.2) = 0.8 - 0.2 = 0.6$.
Step 3. $\langle X\rangle = P(+) - P(-) = 0.5 - 0.5 = 0$.
Step 4. $\langle Y\rangle = P(+i) - P(-i) = 0.9 - 0.1 = 0.8$.

Step 5. Notice $\langle X\rangle^2 + \langle Y\rangle^2 + \langle Z\rangle^2 = 0 + 0.64 + 0.36 = 1$. These three numbers are the coordinates of the state on the Bloch sphere, and for any pure state they lie on the unit sphere (The Qubit and the Bloch Sphere (#/quantum/qubits/bloch-sphere)).

blocks.text: An expectation value is not a possible outcome. Every single $Z$ measurement gives $+1$ or $-1$, never $0.6$. It is the long-run average, and on real hardware it is estimated by repeating the experiment, the subject of the last section.
Degenerate outcomes: projecting onto a subspace

Some observables have repeated eigenvalues. The parity $Z\otimes Z$ of two qubits (the product of their two $Z$ values) is $+1$ on both $\vert00\rangle$ and $\vert11\rangle$ and $-1$ on both $\vert01\rangle$ and $\vert10\rangle$ (Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors (#/quantum/foundations/eigenvalues-and-eigenvectors) works out its eigenspaces). A parity measurement asks only whether the bits agree, not what they are. Its projectors are onto two-dimensional subspaces:
The rules in their general form, valid for degenerate and non-degenerate outcomes alike:

blocks.caption: Projective measurement: probability, and the state after outcome a (projected, then renormalised).

blocks.text: The division renormalises: projecting shortens the vector to length $\sqrt{P(a)}$, and the new state must have length 1. When the outcome is non-degenerate, $\Pi_a\vert\psi\rangle$ is a multiple of $\vert e_a\rangle$, and the rule reduces to collapse onto $\vert e_a\rangle$ up to a phase. When it is degenerate, the superposition inside the eigenspace survives.
Worked example: a parity measurement that creates entanglement

items: Step 1. Start with $\vert\psi\rangle = (\vert00\rangle + \vert01\rangle + \vert11\rangle)/\sqrt3$. Each amplitude is $1/\sqrt3$.
Step 2. $\Pi_{\text{even}}\vert\psi\rangle$ keeps the terms with agreeing bits: $(\vert00\rangle + \vert11\rangle)/\sqrt3$.
Step 3. $P(\text{even}) = \Vert\Pi_{\text{even}}\vert\psi\rangle\Vert^2 = (1 + 1)/3 = 2/3$; $P(\text{odd}) = 1/3$.
Step 4. After the outcome even, renormalise by $\sqrt{2/3}$: $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}(\vert00\rangle + \vert11\rangle)\cdot\sqrt{\frac32} = (\vert00\rangle + \vert11\rangle)/\sqrt2$.

Step 5. That is the Bell state, maximally entangled (Entanglement and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/entanglement)). Neither qubit's value was revealed, and the superposition of $\vert00\rangle$ and $\vert11\rangle$ survived, because both lie in the same eigenspace. A full measurement of both qubits in the computational basis would have destroyed it. Parity measurements like this are how quantum error correction checks for errors without disturbing the encoded information.

blocks.text: Measuring one qubit of two

Measuring only qubit 1 of a pair is another degenerate measurement: outcome 0 does not care what qubit 2 is. Its projector is $\Pi_0 = \vert0\rangle\langle0\vert\otimes I$. Read the $\otimes$ (tensor product) as: the left factor acts on qubit 1 and the right factor on qubit 2, with $I$, the identity, meaning do nothing to qubit 2. So $\Pi_0$ keeps the terms where qubit 1 is 0, whatever qubit 2 is (Composite Systems and Tensor Products (#/quantum/many-body/composite-systems) builds the tensor product properly). Write a general two-qubit state as $\vert\psi\rangle = a\vert00\rangle + b\vert01\rangle + c\vert10\rangle + d\vert11\rangle$. Then:

items: Outcome 0 on qubit 1: $P(0) = \vert a\vert^2 + \vert b\vert^2$, and the state becomes $\vert0\rangle\otimes(a\vert0\rangle + b\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt{\vert a\vert^2 + \vert b\vert^2}$.
Outcome 1 on qubit 1: $P(1) = \vert c\vert^2 + \vert d\vert^2$, and the state becomes $\vert1\rangle\otimes(c\vert0\rangle + d\vert1\rangle)/\sqrt{\vert c\vert^2 + \vert d\vert^2}$.

blocks.text: In words: cross out the terms that disagree with the outcome, then rescale what is left. Qubit 2 ends up in a state that depends on what was found on qubit 1.
Worked example: measuring half of a Bell pair

items: Step 1. $\vert\Phi^+\rangle = (\vert00\rangle + \vert11\rangle)/\sqrt2$: $a = d = 1/\sqrt2$, $b = c = 0$.
Step 2. $P(0) = \frac12$, and the state becomes $\vert0\rangle\otimes\vert0\rangle$. $P(1) = \frac12$, and it becomes $\vert1\rangle\otimes\vert1\rangle$.
Step 3. Before the measurement qubit 2 had no definite value; after it, qubit 2 is certainly equal to qubit 1's result. Measuring qubit 2 next always agrees.

Step 4. Contrast the product state $\vert+\rangle\otimes\vert+\rangle = (\vert00\rangle + \vert01\rangle + \vert10\rangle + \vert11\rangle)/2$: after outcome 0 on qubit 1, qubit 2 is $(\vert0\rangle + \vert1\rangle)/\sqrt2 = \vert+\rangle$, the same as before. With no entanglement, measuring one qubit tells you nothing about the other.

blocks.text: Does this let qubit 1's measurement send a message to qubit 2? No: whoever holds qubit 2 sees 0 or 1 with probability 1/2 each whether or not qubit 1 was measured. The correlation only appears when the two lists of results are compared, which needs ordinary communication. Entanglement and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/entanglement) makes this precise.

blocks.title: Check yourself: partial measurement
blocks.text: Two qubits are in $\frac12\vert00\rangle + \frac12\vert01\rangle + \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\vert11\rangle$. Qubit 1 is measured. Give $P(1)$ and the state of qubit 2 afterwards for each outcome.
blocks.answer: P(1) = 1/2; after 0, qubit 2 is |+⟩; after 1, qubit 2 is |1⟩

blocks.text: Shots: estimating probabilities and expectation values

One run of an experiment gives one outcome. To learn a probability or an expectation value you prepare the same state many times, measure each copy, and count. Each repetition is called a shot. How many shots are enough? The answer comes straight from the binomial distribution (Bernoulli, Binomial and Geometric (#/probability/distributions/binomial-and-geometric)).
The statistics of counting

items: Step 1. Each shot gives outcome 0 with probability $p = P(0)$, independently of the other shots: a Bernoulli trial.
Step 2. In $S$ shots the number of 0s, $K$, follows a binomial distribution: $P(K = k) = \binom{S}{k}p^k(1 - p)^{S - k}$, with mean $Sp$ and variance $Sp(1 - p)$.
Step 3. The natural estimate of $p$ is the fraction $\hat p = K/S$. Its mean is $p$ (it is unbiased) and its variance is $Sp(1 - p)/S^2 = p(1 - p)/S$.
Step 4. For $\langle Z\rangle = P(0) - P(1) = 2p - 1$, average the $\pm1$ outcomes: $\hat z = 2\hat p - 1$. Its variance is $4p(1 - p)/S$.

Step 5. Rewrite in terms of $\langle Z\rangle$: since $p = (1 + \langle Z\rangle)/2$, $4p(1 - p) = (1 + \langle Z\rangle)(1 - \langle Z\rangle) = 1 - \langle Z\rangle^2$. This is the variance of a single $\pm1$ outcome.

blocks.caption: Standard error of a ±1 average from S shots.

blocks.text: The standard error $\sigma$ (the square root of the variance) is the typical size of the error in the estimate. For large $S$ the central limit theorem (The Central Limit Theorem (#/probability/limit-theorems/central-limit-theorem)) makes $\hat z$ nearly normal, so the estimate lands within $\pm1.96\sigma$ of the truth about 95% of the time. The bound $1/\sqrt S$ is the worst case, reached when $\langle Z\rangle = 0$ and every shot is a fair coin; a state with $\langle Z\rangle = \pm1$ gives the same outcome every time and needs one shot.
Worked example: how good is 1000 shots?

items: Step 1. Suppose $p = 0.7$, so $\langle Z\rangle = 0.4$. Single-shot variance $1 - 0.4^2 = 0.84$.

Step 4. How likely is an error bigger than 0.05? An error of 0.05 in $\hat z$ is $0.025$ in $\hat p$, which is 25 counts out of 1000. The exact binomial probability that $K$ is outside 675 to 725 is 0.078; the normal approximation gives 0.084. So about one run in thirteen misses by more than 0.05.
Step 5. To halve the error you need four times the shots; for one more decimal digit, a hundred times. This $1/\sqrt S$ law is the single most important cost in quantum experiments.

blocks.text: The code sample below estimates $\langle Z\rangle$ for the state $\sqrt{0.7}\vert0\rangle + \sqrt{0.3}\vert1\rangle$ (exact $\langle Z\rangle = 0.4$) with increasing shot counts, and then runs the collapse experiment from earlier.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
# Born rule: measure s = 0.3 written as sqrt(1-s)|0> + sqrt(s)|1>, with S shots.
s = 0.3
psi = np.array([np.sqrt(1 - s), np.sqrt(s)])
p = np.abs(psi) ** 2
for S in (10, 100, 1000, 10000):
    z = 1 - 2 * rng.choice([0, 1], size=S, p=p)    # Z eigenvalue: +1 for |0>, -1 for |1>
    print(f"S={S:6d}: <Z> estimate = {z.mean():+.4f}, standard error {np.sqrt((1 - (1 - 2*s)**2) / S):.4f}")
print("exact <Z> =", round(1 - 2 * s, 4))
# Collapse: measure Z, then X, then Z again on one copy, many times over.
plus, minus = np.array([1, 1]) / np.sqrt(2), np.array([1, -1]) / np.sqrt(2)
basisZ, basisX = [np.array([1., 0]), np.array([0., 1])], [plus, minus]
def measure(state, basis):
    probs = [abs(b @ state) ** 2 for b in basis]
    k = rng.choice(2, p=probs)
    return k, basis[k]                             # outcome and post-measurement state
same, flipped = 0, 0
for _ in range(10000):
    k1, st = measure(psi, basisZ); k1b, st = measure(st, basisZ)   # repeat Z: always agrees
    same += (k1 == k1b)
    _, st = measure(st, basisX); k3, _ = measure(st, basisZ)      # X in between: Z is re-randomised
    flipped += (k3 != k1)
print(f"Z then Z again: agreed in {same} of 10000 runs")
print(f"Z, then X, then Z: second Z differed from the first in {flipped/100:.1f}% of runs")

blocks.text: Output of the run, for $s = 0.3$ (exact $\langle Z\rangle = 0.4$): the estimate is $+0.40$ at 10 shots (standard error 0.29, so the agreement is luck), $+0.34$ at 100 (0.092), $+0.378$ at 1000 (0.029) and $+0.3974$ at 10 000 (0.0092). Repeating a $Z$ measurement agreed in all 10 000 runs; with an $X$ measurement in between, the second $Z$ differed from the first in 49.1% of runs.

widget.title: Estimating an expectation value from shots

blocks.text: Try this: the jagged line is the running average of simulated $\pm1$ outcomes; it wanders early and then stays mostly inside the shrinking band of one standard error (about two-thirds of the time, as a normal distribution predicts). Change the seed to replay a different run of the same experiment. Set θ to 0 (the state $\vert0\rangle$): measuring $Z$ gives $+1$ every time and the band collapses to the line, while switching to $X$ gives the widest band of all, a fair coin. Raising the shots from 500 to 5000 makes the band at the right-hand end narrower only by a factor of about 3 ($\sqrt{10} = 3.16$): with θ = 60 and $Z$ its half-width goes from 0.039 to 0.012.

blocks.title: Check yourself: shot budget
blocks.text: A $\pm1$ observable has $\langle A\rangle = 0$. How many shots give a standard error of 0.02? And of 0.002?
solution: Ten times smaller error needs $100\times$ the shots: $250\,000$.

blocks.text: Putting it together: planning a Y measurement

You want to measure $\langle Y\rangle$ of the state $\vert s\rangle = \sqrt{0.8}\vert0\rangle + i\sqrt{0.2}\vert1\rangle$ on hardware that only measures $Z$, to a standard error of 0.01. What circuit do you run, what do you expect to see, and how many shots do you need?

items: Step 1. Circuit: prepare $\vert s\rangle$, apply $S^\dagger$ then $H_d$, measure. Outcome 0 means $+i$ (report $+1$); outcome 1 means $-i$ (report $-1$).
Step 2. Expected frequencies, from the worked example: outcome 0 with probability 0.9, outcome 1 with probability 0.1. So $\langle Y\rangle = 0.9 - 0.1 = 0.8$.
Step 3. Single-shot variance: $1 - 0.8^2 = 0.36$.
Step 5. Sanity check against the worst case: a state with $\langle Y\rangle = 0$ would need $10\,000$ shots. The more predictable the outcome, the fewer shots an average needs.

Step 6. Had you forgotten the $S^\dagger$ and applied only $H_d$, you would have measured $X$ and found $\langle X\rangle = 0$: a correct answer to the wrong question. Checking the basis rotation is the first thing to do when a hardware result looks off.

blocks.text: Key points

items: Born rule: in an orthonormal basis $\{\vert e_k\rangle\}$, $P(k) = \vert\langle e_k\vert\psi\rangle\vert^2 = \langle\psi\vert\Pi_k\vert\psi\rangle$; the probabilities add to 1 by the resolution of the identity.
Collapse: after outcome $k$ the state is $\vert e_k\rangle$. Repeating the same measurement agrees; measuring in another basis in between scrambles the result.
To measure in the basis $\{\vert e_k\rangle\}$ with a $Z$ detector, apply $U$ with $U\vert e_k\rangle = \vert k\rangle$ first: $H_d$ for $X$, $H_dS^\dagger$ for $Y$.
Measuring an observable $A = \sum_a a\Pi_a$ reports an eigenvalue; the average is $\langle A\rangle = \langle\psi\vert A\vert\psi\rangle$.
Degenerate outcomes project onto a subspace and renormalise: $\vert\psi\rangle \to \Pi_a\vert\psi\rangle/\sqrt{P(a)}$; superpositions inside the subspace survive.
Measuring one qubit of an entangled pair changes the state of the other; measuring one qubit of a product state does not.
With $S$ shots the standard error of a $\pm1$ average is $\sqrt{(1 - \langle A\rangle^2)/S} \le 1/\sqrt S$: four times the shots halves the error.

blocks.text: Problems

blocks.title: Probabilities in two bases
blocks.text: For $\vert\psi\rangle = \sqrt{0.7}\,\vert0\rangle + \sqrt{0.3}\,\vert1\rangle$, give $P(1)$ in the computational basis and $P(+)$ in the $X$ basis.

blocks.title: Shots for a target precision
blocks.text: A feature has $\langle Z\rangle = 0.4$. How many shots give a standard error of 0.01?

blocks.title: Measuring one qubit of two
blocks.text: Two qubits are in $(\vert00\rangle + \vert01\rangle + \vert11\rangle)/\sqrt3$. Qubit 1 is measured and gives 0. What is the state afterwards, and what is $P(0)$ for that first measurement?
solution: Keep the terms with qubit 1 equal to 0: $\vert00\rangle + \vert01\rangle$, with total weight $2/3$. So $P(0) = 2/3$.
Renormalise: $(\vert00\rangle + \vert01\rangle)/\sqrt2 = \vert0\rangle\otimes\vert+\rangle$. Qubit 2 is now in $\vert+\rangle$, which it was not before the measurement.

blocks.title: Post-measurement state in the X basis
blocks.text: The state $\vert s\rangle = \sqrt{0.8}\vert0\rangle + i\sqrt{0.2}\vert1\rangle$ is measured in the $X$ basis, giving $-$. It is then measured in the computational basis. What is $P(0)$ now, and how does it compare with $P(0)$ before?
blocks.hint: After the measurement the state is the basis state of the outcome.
solution: The $X$ measurement erased the information about $Z$, exactly as in the $Z$, $X$, $Z$ sequence.

blocks.title: A parity measurement on a product state
blocks.text: Two qubits are in $\vert+\rangle\otimes\vert+\rangle$. Their parity $Z\otimes Z$ is measured and gives odd. What is the state afterwards? Is it entangled?
blocks.hint: Keep the terms whose two bits differ.
solution: Renormalise by $\sqrt{1/2}$: $(\vert01\rangle + \vert10\rangle)/\sqrt2$, the Bell state $\vert\Psi^+\rangle$, which is entangled. A measurement that reveals only a joint property of two qubits can entangle them.

blocks.title: Probability of a misleading estimate
blocks.text: A state has $\langle X\rangle = 0$. With 100 shots, roughly how likely is the estimate to come out at $0.1$ or more in size (that is, $\vert\hat x\vert \ge 0.1$)?
solution: $\vert\hat x\vert \ge 0.1$ is one standard error or more. For a normal distribution that has probability about 0.32.

Exactly: $\hat x = 2K/100 - 1$ and $\vert\hat x\vert < 0.1$ means $K$ from 46 to 54, whose binomial probability is 0.632; that is $\hat x = \pm0.08$ at most, so $\vert\hat x\vert \ge 0.1$ has probability $0.368$. (The normal estimate 0.32 is close; counts are whole numbers, which is why they differ.)
So about a third of 100-shot experiments would suggest a non-zero $\langle X\rangle$ of 0.1 or more when it is really zero.
blocks.answer: about 1 in 3 (0.37 exactly, 0.32 from the normal approximation)

blocks.text: Where this is used

items: Every feature $\operatorname{Tr}(Z_i\rho)$ on the QRC shelf is an expectation value, estimated from shots on hardware: Measurement Back-Action and Shot Noise (#/qrc/hardware/measurement-back-action).

Collapse is why a reservoir cannot simply be measured at every step and continue: the restart, weak-measurement and partial-measurement protocols of Online Measurement Protocols (#/qrc/hardware/online-protocols) all work around it.
The general (POVM) form of measurement, including weak measurement, is on the QRC shelf's Measurement (#/qrc/open-systems/measurement) page.
